newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq to rebut UN on banned missiles, official says.
newsitem.headline: Iraq to rebut UN on banned missiles, official says.

text.p: A senior Iraqi official was quoted on Sunday as saying that Iraq is gathering evidence to counter U.N. statements about the existence of banned missiles in its arsenal.

General Amer Hammoudi al-Saadi, an adviser at the presidential office, did not say in the newspaper remarks whether Iraq would heed a U.N. demand to have missile parts analysed by international experts in the United States.
The U.N. Security Council censured Iraq late last year for refusing to allow more than 100 missile engines to be taken abroad for examination by experts.

The U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction under the terms of the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire, has most of the parts packed in boxes ready for shipment abroad. The rest are stored in warehouses in Baghdad under strict U.N. surveillance.

Saadi said Iraq had a clear idea of UNSCOM's claims and "this would help us work in a scientific and documented manner to refute them by supplying the international community with convincing material evidence proving that Iraq is telling the truth," the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya reported.
"General Saadi...confirmed that Iraq is continuing with its full and objective cooperation with UNSCOM and the long-term (arms) monitoring centre in Baghdad," it said.
"Everybody knows that Iraq is telling the truth and we do not hide anything and UNSCOM could not condemn Iraq in a direct form or in a scientific and documented manner," Saadi told the newspaper.

UNSCOM chairman Rolf Ekeus reported during his December visit to Baghdad that he believed Iraq still had "a significant number of operational missiles which could constitute a complete missile force".
Ekeus's ballistic missile experts say they still lack a full accounting of rockets with a range greater than 150 km (95 miles) which Baghdad is banned from possessing or manufacturing.
Ekeus is due in Baghdad in February in the latest bid to persuade Iraqi leaders to allow the parts be taken abroad.
